source.title: CANARY: Zero-Label Detection of Fine-Tuning Contamination in Language Models

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes models with harmful or benign data and measures harmful output under generation-based evaluation, but uses a contamination setup and LDA-based measures rather than the original fine-tuning recipe and measure.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports checkpoint-detection AUROCs, SAE feature activations, attack robustness, prompt-prioritization results, and perplexity. Those are not rows here because they do not measure the claim versions’ named behaviour. Harmful output rates under LDA, benign fine-tuning output results, and the reported generation-mode comparison are included.
record.test_reason: A detection paper: it cites Qi et al. as the threat and reports its detector's performance. Fine-tuning starts from pretrained base checkpoints (Fig. 1 labels the base 'pre-trained'; Fig. 8 says 'Base model (untuned)'), not safety-trained models. So no row measures removal or erosion of safety. Harm rates are in-domain harmful medical advice, the trained content itself, mostly elicited under LDA amplification as an output-level detector baseline.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that harmful fine-tuning contamination shifts hidden-state geometry before it appears in outputs; they say output methods see nothing below 7.5%. They present CANARY as a zero-label detector (AUROC 1.000 at 1%) that is harm-specific and robust to style and gradient-noise attacks. They also present SAE-filtered amplification, prompt prioritization and feature suppression (70% to 10% harm) as a governance pipeline.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses contamination of fine-tuning data with synthetic harmful medical advice mixed with benign examples, then evaluates outputs using LDA and SAE-based generation; it does not report the original study's fine-tuning recipe or example counts.
record.method_sensitivity: Output-level results differ by contamination rate; the paper reports no generation-based signal below 7.5%. Generation-mode choice changes the reported harm rate. Other reported detector sensitivities include model architecture and layer, but those results concern detection rather than the claim's behavioural outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning a pretrained base on 7.5–20% harmful medical advice yields 13.3–26.7% max harm under LDA. Benign-persona and random-token mixes yield 0.0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful data contamination of fine-tuning of a non-safety-trained base produces in-domain harmful outputs detectable by amplified generation above a threshold rate.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-filtered generation surfaces 33.3% peak harm versus 6.7% for original LDA on contaminated M1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden-state SAE-filtered amplification elicits latent fine-tuned harm more effectively than logit-space LDA.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing 16 SAE features at inference cuts greedy harm from 70% to 10% on M1 at r=5%, with perplexity unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning-induced harmful behaviour is concentrated in a small SAE activation subspace that can be suppressed at inference.

record.code_released: Code, experiment scripts, and trained SAE weights will be released upon publication.
record.problems: The behavioural output evaluation is reported for M1, not across all four model pairs. The text gives contamination percentages but not fine-tuning example counts, and does not state that the tested checkpoint was safety-trained. Several output rates come from a discrete 30-prompt set. The paper does not provide a direct ordinary-generation baseline for the low-contamination behavioural claim.
record.rows_left_out: Checkpoint AUROC and detection-limit results (§5.1–§5.3, §5.6–§5.9), feature activation ratios (§5.5, Figure 7), and attack-robustness AUROCs (§5.7, Table 4) were left out because they measure detection or feature geometry rather than the listed harmful-compliance behaviours. Random-token fine-tuning output results in Table 2 were left out because random noise is not benign instruction data.

untested.parts: No safety-trained starting model; harm is in-domain trained content, not compliance with general harmful requests.
The benign persona fine-tune starts from a pretrained base, so there is no safety to erode.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attack on a safety-trained model's refusal.
No weight or rank localization of safety.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1/V2 labels were wrong: the models fine-tuned are pretrained base checkpoints, so safety removal or erosion cannot be assessed. The paper is internally inconsistent: it claims no output signal below 7.5%, yet Fig. 9 reports 70% greedy harm at r=5% versus 0% for the clean baseline. The harm prompts are in-domain medical prompts, a 30-prompt set. M4 'RLHF' refers to the fine-tuning paradigm, and no harm rates are given for M2–M4.

versions.untested_parts: The paper gives contamination percentages, not counts of fine-tuning examples; it does not establish that the tested checkpoints were safety-trained, and its output results are for LDA amplification rather than ordinary generation.
The benign condition is a legal-persona shift, not ordinary benign instruction data; the reported output evaluation is under LDA.
Per-token KL by response position is not measured.
The paper tests LDA and SAE-filtered generation modes, but not compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or other decoding changes.
The paper suppresses SAE activation features, not a small set of weights or ranks.
The paper does not test whether a particular dataset or training objective causes safety to be shallow.
The paper does not train to spread safety across response positions or test whether such training holds up.

rows.check: An inference-time SAE feature-suppression mitigation (the study's own method), not weight or rank localization. The 70% baseline is greedy harm on contaminated M1 at r=5%.
